source.title: Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Miles Wang; Tom Dupré la Tour; Olivia Watkins; Aleksandar Makelov; Ryan A. Chi; Samuel Miserendino; Johannes Heidecke; Tejal Patwardhan; Daniel P. Mossing

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure data are available only as figures, and some extracted figure/table layout is garbled.
record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE feature analysis and interventions to GPT-4o and examines whether recoverable features relate to behavior in an LLM. It does not test toy-model superposition or its capacity geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many misalignment, fine-tuning, and reward-hacking results that do not test the claim versions. The included rows concern SAE features recovered and analyzed in GPT-4o. The study does not test superposition, feature-capacity competition, or whether SAE features are canonical units.
record.test_reason: The study uses a pretrained GPT-4o SAE as a model-diffing tool. It reports what that tool finds about emergent misalignment: persona latents, steering effects and classification AUROCs. It does not measure whether features are superposed, spread across neurons, or recoverable by SAEs as a claim in itself. It runs no reconstruction or feature-count analysis and no comparison with a neuron basis. The SAE's ability to recover features is assumed, not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The paper's main conclusions are behavioural: emergent misalignment arises across SFT domains, RL and helpful-only models, and grows with model size. Small benign fine-tunes re-align models. SAE model-diffing found misaligned-persona latents, especially a toxic persona (#10), that steer and predict misalignment. The authors call SAEs a positive update but note the auditing setting was easy and their understanding of latents' links to behaviour is limited.
record.recipe_differences: This study uses a pretrained SAE to compare GPT-4o activations before and after fine-tuning, then steers SAE decoder directions and measures behavior. It does not reproduce the toy-network feature-training or geometry measurements in the original source.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering strength was selected subject to an incoherence threshold; the main analysis used evaluation prompts that elicit known misalignment. The authors note that rankings/classification are more discriminative with evaluation prompts than with unrelated Alpaca prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Single SAE latents from a base-model SAE on GPT-4o (2.1M latents, k=64, middle layer) transfer to the post-trained and fine-tuned models. Steering along them induces or suppresses broad misalignment, and their activation discriminates aligned from misaligned models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individual SAE dictionary directions in frontier LLMs are causally relevant handles on high-level behaviours and transfer across fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: The top misalignment latents are pairwise more correlated than random latents (cosine up to 0.34) but not equivalent (Fig. 25).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents tied to one behaviour form a cluster of related but distinct directions.

record.problems: The SAE analysis is centered on GPT-4o and one middle layer. Latent interpretation is based partly on inspecting activating examples and auto-interpretations. The method uses known misalignment prompts for its main discovery and causal-testing steps. Steering results are subject to an incoherence threshold, and several relevant plotted values are not stated numerically in the text. The paper does not test capacity competition, superposition geometry, feature completeness, or canonicality.
record.rows_left_out: Other SAE steering latents and further feature-classifier analyses are not separately listed; they are not needed to represent the reported evidence for V4. Many non-SAE misalignment results in Sections 2 and 4 and appendices do not bear on the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis of polysemanticity.
All: no analysis of neuron polysemanticity.
No measure of features spread across neurons. SAE recovery is assumed rather than evaluated, with no reconstruction or comparison with a neuron basis.
No test of completeness, stability across SAEs, or canonicality. Only one SAE and one middle layer are used.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is dropped. Finding interpretable, causally useful latents with an SAE presupposes that SAEs recover features; it does not test whether LLMs store features in superposition. The study cites Toy Models only as background to the sparse coding hypothesis.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from capacity pressure or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study analyzes SAE features in GPT-4o, but does not measure feature distribution across neurons or compare SAE recovery with other feature representations.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the model.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Used an SAE trained on GPT-4o base-model activations to identify and interpret latents associated with misalignment.
rows.measure: Qualitative interpretability of the strongest SAE latents for steering misalignment
rows.value: The authors interpret ten latents, including toxic persona, sarcastic advice, sarcasm/satire, and sarcasm in fiction; they report that the latents are correlated to varying degrees but not equivalent.
rows.note: This bears on recovery of interpretable SAE features in GPT-4o, not on whether these features are complete or canonical.
rows.check: Qualitative interpretation of ten selected latents found by the study's own pipeline. It is a tool output, not a measure of feature distribution or SAE recovery as such.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Added a multiple of the SAE latent #10 decoder vector to token activations to steer toward the toxic-persona latent.

conditions.value: positive; strength selected subject to incoherence ≤ 10%

rows.note: The authors state that positive steering induces misalignment in the original GPT-4o model; the plotted values are not available as text.
rows.check: Positive steering with latent #10 measures misalignment caused by the study's own method. Values are figure-only. No version names this behaviour.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.stage_stated: post-trained and fine-tuned on incorrect advice or insecure code
rows.operation_detail: Added a negative multiple of SAE latent #10 to token activations to steer away from the toxic-persona latent.

conditions.value: negative; strength selected subject to incoherence ≤ 10%

rows.note: The text says negative steering suppresses misalignment and that the selected latents work robustly across multiple misaligned models.
rows.check: Negative steering suppresses misalignment. This is the study's own method's performance. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean activation change of SAE latent #10 after fine-tuning across the examined datasets.
rows.measure: Whether latent activation increase discriminates aligned from misaligned models
rows.value: The text reports perfect discrimination across the fine-tuning data domains examined.
rows.note: This is evidence that an SAE latent’s activation change tracks the study’s aligned/misaligned model distinction; it is not a general test of SAE feature completeness.
rows.check: Latent #10 activation change discriminating aligned from misaligned models is a detection result, not a superposition or SAE-recovery measure.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Used SAE latent #10 activation to classify persona-jailbreak prompts.

conditions.value: persona jailbreaks versus benign prompts; persona versus non-persona jailbreaks
OpenAI o3-mini judged whether prompts were persona jailbreaks

rows.value: AUROC = 0.96 versus benign prompts; 0.93 versus non-persona jailbreak prompts.
rows.note: The feature activation discriminated the prompt categories in this evaluation.
rows.check: AUROC 0.96/0.93 for classifying persona jailbreaks measures the latent as a classifier. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Steered with individual SAE latents and evaluated different misalignment behavior categories.
rows.measure: Misalignment profile, including illegal recommendations and factual incorrectness
rows.value: The text reports that steering with latent #10 caused more illegal recommendations, but not more factual incorrectness.
rows.note: The text gives this as an example of distinct SAE latents relating to different behavior profiles.
rows.check: Behaviour profile under steering with latent #10 is the method's output, not a claim-version measure.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Steered with SAE latent #31 and evaluated different misalignment behavior categories.
rows.value: The text identifies latent #31 as a direction that can cause factual incorrectness.
rows.note: The text contrasts this effect with latent #10’s effect on illegal recommendations.
rows.check: Behaviour profile under steering with latent #31 is the method's output, not a claim-version measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
